operations.evidence: For domestic gas duties, HSE describes a landlord as someone renting property under a lease shorter than seven years or under a licence.
Other legislation may use a different landlord definition, and legal status cannot be inferred from parcel ownership alone.
Landlord gas-safety duties cover a broad range of rented accommodation, including local-authority, housing-association, private, hostel, bed-sit, hotel and holiday accommodation.
The listed examples do not prove that a specific tenancy falls within scope.
Landlords are responsible for tenant safety under the Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998 for gas appliances, fittings and flues they provide.
A general statutory duty is not evidence of compliance or non-compliance at a named property.
Gas appliances, fittings and flues in communal areas that tenants may use are included in landlord duties.
Communal-area coverage does not identify which installations exist in a specific building.
Where a contract gives an agent responsibility, the same relevant gas-safety duties apply to that agent.
Contractual allocation must be established from the actual agreement and cannot be assumed.
Maintenance and repair of landlord-provided gas pipework, appliances and flues must be arranged through a Gas Safe registered engineer.
The requirement does not prove that a named engineer or installation is registered or compliant.
Landlords must arrange a gas-safety check every 12 months by a Gas Safe registered engineer.
An annual interval does not establish the date or result of a specific property's latest check.
The 2018 amendment allows an annual gas-safety check in the two months before its due date while retaining the existing expiry date.
The flexibility does not extend the maximum statutory cycle beyond the permitted schedule.
Landlords must keep gas-safety check records for two years.
A retention duty does not prove that records exist or are complete for a named tenancy.
A copy of the gas-safety record must be issued to each existing tenant within 28 days of the check.
The deadline cannot be evaluated without the actual check and delivery dates.
New tenants must receive a copy of the gas-safety record before moving in.
The duty does not establish whether a particular tenant received the document.
For a tenant-owned gas appliance not supplied by the landlord, the landlord retains duties for associated installation pipework but not the appliance itself.
Ownership and installation boundaries require property-specific evidence.
A landlord within a larger building should ensure communal gas appliances, flues and pipework are maintained and checked by the building owner and that evidence is available.
The guidance does not prove that building-owner evidence has been obtained for a specific block.
HSE states that where a lease is longer than seven years and for life, the landlord is not responsible for gas-safety checks and maintenance under this duty.
Lease duration and legal form must be confirmed from the actual lease.
HSE states that the 2018 timing changes do not relax regulatory requirements or reduce safety standards.
The statement is about the amendment and does not certify any individual installation.
The asbestos dutyholder in non-domestic premises may be the building owner, landlord or person or organisation clearly responsible for maintenance or repair.
Dutyholder identity depends on legal responsibility and cannot be assigned from address data alone.
A tenancy agreement or contract can allocate responsibility for maintenance or repair and therefore affect the asbestos duty.
The allocation must be read from the actual agreement.
In multi-occupied buildings, asbestos responsibilities may be shared between owners and occupiers for different parts.
Shared responsibility cannot be spatially inferred without contractual evidence.
A managing agent acts for the owner but does not assume the owner's legal asbestos duties; ultimate responsibility remains with the owner.
Agency arrangements still require document-level verification.
The asbestos register is a live document that must contain current information on the presence and condition of asbestos-containing materials.
Register existence or freshness cannot be inferred from building age.
The asbestos register records known and presumed asbestos-containing materials.
Presumption is a management control and not laboratory confirmation.
A management survey is intended to enable the dutyholder to produce an asbestos register and management plan for normal occupation and use.
A management survey is not automatically suitable for refurbishment or demolition work.
A management survey should inspect internal, concealed, external and maintenance-disturbance areas described by HSE.
Actual survey coverage must be checked against plans, access limitations and the report.
Restrictions imposed on survey scope can seriously undermine the value and usefulness of an asbestos survey.
The presence of a caveat does not by itself quantify the resulting risk.
HSE states that obtaining and analysing a sample is the only way to confirm whether suspect material contains asbestos fibres.
A visual suspicion remains unconfirmed until competent sampling and analysis occur.
Sampling asbestos materials should be carried out by a suitably trained person, with a competent surveyor used when in doubt.
Training or competence cannot be inferred from a company name alone.
Asbestos samples must be analysed by trained and competent analysts using accredited laboratories, with UKAS providing accreditation listings.
Accreditation status must be checked for the specific laboratory and relevant scope.
An asbestos management plan should identify who is responsible for managing asbestos, including deputies.
Named responsibility in a plan does not prove that assigned actions were performed.
The plan should include the asbestos register, a site plan showing ACM locations and uninspected areas, and a schedule for monitoring ACM condition.
Planned monitoring does not establish current ACM condition without inspection evidence.
The asbestos management plan must be communicated to site or building managers, employees, contractors and maintenance workers who may disturb asbestos.
A published plan does not prove that every relevant person received or understood it.
The guidance applies in England to relevant private and social rented homes, subject to listed exclusions.
Regulatory scope cannot be assigned without tenancy-specific evidence.
